title: Health check
privacy: Your answers are private. Only you, and the experts you choose, can see them.

about.name: About you
about.title: A little about you
about.sub: These change how your results are worked out.
why: Healthy ranges and risk scores differ by age and sex, so we need both to give you accurate results.
Pregnancy changes what's healthy for weight, food and activity, so we handle it differently.

body.name: Body
body.title: Your height and weight
body.sub: Use your most recent measurements. A rough number is fine, and you can update it any time.
why: BMI compares your weight with your height. It's a quick first check, but it doesn't know about muscle, age or body shape.
That's why we also ask for your waist. Fat around the middle is linked to diabetes and heart disease, even at a healthy weight. A good rule: keep your waist to less than half your height.

eating.name: Eating
eating.title: How do you usually eat?
eating.sub: Choose the answer closest to a typical week.
why: WHO recommends at least 5 portions (400 g) of fruit and vegetables a day, less than 5 g of salt (about one teaspoon), and keeping added sugar low.
Your answers help us suggest easy swaps with foods you already cook, not a foreign diet.

activity.name: Activity and sleep
activity.title: How active are you, and how do you sleep?
activity.sub: Think about a normal week, not your best or worst one.
why: WHO recommends adults get 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening on at least 2 days.
Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Too little affects appetite, blood sugar and mood.

habits.name: Habits
habits.title: Tobacco and alcohol
habits.sub: Be as honest as you can. Nobody else sees these answers.
why: Tobacco in any form is one of the biggest causes of heart disease, stroke and cancer, and stopping helps at any age.
WHO advises that less alcohol is always better for health, and that no amount is completely safe.

mind.name: Mind and mood
mind.title: How have you been feeling lately?
mind.sub: Your answers stay private. Only you, and the experts you choose, can see them.
why: These four questions are the PHQ-2 and GAD-2, short screening questions that doctors around the world use to spot low mood and anxiety early.
They can't diagnose anything. They help us know when to suggest extra support.

history.name: Health history
history.title: Your health history
history.sub: This helps us spot risks early and keep your plan safe for you.
why: These questions come from FINDRISC, a validated score that estimates the chance of developing type 2 diabetes in the next 10 years.
Blood pressure is grouped using the International Society of Hypertension's 2020 guideline.

about.ageHint: You need to be 18 or over.
about.ageError: Please enter an age between 18 and 110.
about.sexHint: Healthy waist sizes and risk scores are different for women and men.

body.waistHow: Measure halfway between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, after breathing out normally. Don't pull the tape tight.
body.rangeError: Please check your height and weight. They look outside the usual range.
body.liveEmpty: Enter your height and weight to see your BMI straight away.
body.pregnancyNote: During pregnancy, BMI isn't used to judge your weight. Enter your current measurements; your dietitian will guide the rest.

eating.answered: questions answered. There are no wrong answers; think about a normal week.

fv.title: Portions of fruit and vegetables on a typical day
fv.help: A portion is about a handful: one orange or banana, or a cupful of cooked ugu, spinach or garden egg.

drinks.title: How often do you have sugary drinks?
drinks.help: Soft drinks, malt drinks, sweetened juice or zobo, or tea and coffee with sugar.

cubes.title: Seasoning or stock cubes in your cooking each day
cubes.help: Cubes are one of the biggest hidden sources of salt.

fried.title: How often do you eat fried food?
fried.help: Such as puff-puff, akara, fried plantain, yam or chicken.

grains.title: Which grains do you mostly eat?
grains.help: Whole grains: ofada or brown rice, oats, whole wheat. Refined: white rice, white bread, pasta.

activity.minutes: Active minutes in a typical week
activity.minutesHelp: Anything that makes you breathe faster but still able to talk: brisk walking, dancing, cycling, sweeping, farm work.

bands.grow: Room to grow: {{gap}} minutes to go

activity.strength: Days a week you do muscle-strengthening activity
activity.strengthHelp: Such as squats, push-ups, carrying loads or lifting weights.
activity.sleep: Hours of sleep on a typical night

tobacco.title: Do you smoke or use tobacco?
tobacco.help: Including cigarettes, shisha, snuff or chewing tobacco.

alcohol.title: How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
alcohol.help: One drink is a small bottle of beer, a glass of wine or palm wine, or a shot of spirits.

intro.title: Know where you stand, in about 5 minutes.
intro.body: Answer seven short sections about your body, food, activity, sleep and wellbeing. We'll turn your answers into your Living Score and a plan built around you.
intro.stopAnyTime: You can stop and continue later
intro.standards: Built on World Health Organization guidance and validated tools used by doctors worldwide (FINDRISC, PHQ-2, GAD-2). This check is a guide, not a diagnosis.

score.title: Your Living Score
score.body: One number from 0 to 100, across six areas of health.

numbers.title: Your key numbers
numbers.body: BMI, waist-to-height ratio, blood pressure and type 2 diabetes risk.

priorities.title: Your top 3 priorities
priorities.body: Small, specific changes using foods you already know.

results.numbersIntro: Each one is compared with international guidelines, so you know exactly where you stand.

bmi.label: Body mass index (BMI)

notes.underweight: Below the healthy range of 18.5 to 24.9. A dietitian can help you gain weight in a healthy way.
notes.healthy: Within the healthy range of 18.5 to 24.9. Keep it up.
notes.overweight: A little above the healthy range of 18.5 to 24.9. Losing about {{kg}} kg would bring you closer.
notes.obesity: Above the healthy range. Losing even 5% of your weight (about {{kg}} kg) lowers the risk of diabetes and heart disease.

bmi.pregnant: During pregnancy, BMI isn't used to judge weight. Your dietitian will guide you.

whtr.label: Waist-to-height ratio

notes.healthy: Your waist ({{waist}} cm) is less than half your height. That's healthy.
notes.increased: Your waist ({{waist}} cm) is just over half your height. Aim for under {{target}} cm.
notes.high: Your waist ({{waist}} cm) is well over half your height, which raises health risks. Aim for under {{target}} cm.

whtr.missing: Add your waist size to see this. It's one of the best signs of health risk.

bp.label: Blood pressure
bp.missing: Not measured yet. Most pharmacies can check it in minutes.

notes.normal: Below 130/85, which is normal. Check it again every year.
notes.highNormal: Slightly raised. Less salt and more activity help. Check again within 3 to 6 months.
notes.grade1: In the high blood pressure range. Please see a doctor or nurse to check it again soon.
notes.grade2: Very high. Please see a doctor within the next week.
notes.crisis: Dangerously high. Please get medical help today.

findrisc.label: Type 2 diabetes risk
findrisc.note: About {{risk}} people with this score develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years.
findrisc.noteLow: About {{risk}} people with this score develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years. Keep it that way.
findrisc.noWaist: Add your waist size for a more accurate score.
findrisc.notApplicable: You've told us you have diabetes or prediabetes, so this risk score doesn't apply. Your plan will be tailored to it.

results.prioritiesIntro: Start with one. Small changes you keep beat big changes you don't.

vegetables.title: Add more vegetables and fruit every day
vegetables.body: You have about {{now}} of the 5 portions WHO recommends. Stir ugu or spinach into your stew, snack on garden egg or an orange, and add vegetables to rice.

moveMore.title: Build up to 150 active minutes a week
moveMore.body: You're at about {{minutes}}. A brisk 20-minute walk after dinner on a few evenings would close the {{gap}}-minute gap.

sugaryDrinks.title: Swap one sugary drink a day
sugaryDrinks.body: Try water with lemon, unsweetened zobo, or tea without sugar. It's one of the quickest ways to lower diabetes risk.

lessSalt.title: Use fewer seasoning cubes
lessSalt.body: Cubes are packed with salt. Try one less, and add flavour with onions, garlic, ginger, crayfish or fresh pepper.

lessFried.title: Boil, grill or steam more often
lessFried.body: Swap some fried plantain or akara for boiled plantain or moi moi. You'll keep the taste and lose a lot of oil.

wholeGrains.title: Choose whole grains
wholeGrains.body: Ofada or brown rice, oats and whole-wheat bread keep you full longer and steady your blood sugar.

strength.title: Add strength exercises twice a week
strength.body: Squats, push-ups against a wall, or carrying loads all count. Ten minutes is a good start.

sleep.title: Protect your sleep
sleep.body: You sleep about {{hours}} hours. Try a regular bedtime, less screen time before bed, and less caffeine after midday.

alcohol.title: Cut down on alcohol
alcohol.body: Try alcohol-free days each week and smaller measures. Your blood pressure, sleep and weight will all benefit.

weight.title: Aim to lose about {{kg}} kg
weight.body: That's about 5% of your weight, gently, over a few months. It's enough to lower your risk of diabetes and heart disease.

stopSmoking.title: Get support to stop smoking
stopSmoking.body: It's the single best thing you can do for your health, at any age. Support makes it far more likely to work.

talkToSomeone.title: Talk to someone about how you've been feeling
talkToSomeone.body: Your answers suggest things may be hard right now. A psychologist can help, by video, voice or chat, in private.

keepGoing.title: Keep doing what you're doing
keepGoing.body: You're meeting the main guidelines. Check again in 4 weeks to keep it that way.

salt.target: Under 5 g of salt a day

mind.positive: Your answers suggest you may be dealing with low mood or anxiety. That's more common than you might think, and talking to someone really helps.
mind.negative: Your answers don't suggest low mood or anxiety right now. That's worth protecting: sleep, movement and time with people all help.
mind.skipped: You chose not to answer these questions. You can talk to a psychologist any time, no questionnaire needed.
mind.crisis: If you're thinking of harming yourself, please call 112 now or go to the nearest hospital.

checks.bpDoctor: Your blood pressure is high. Please book a check with a doctor or nurse soon.
checks.bpRecheck: Your blood pressure is slightly raised. Check it again within 3 to 6 months.
checks.bpUnknown: You don't know your blood pressure. Most pharmacies can check it in a few minutes; add it next time.
checks.sugarTestSoon: Your diabetes risk is raised. A fasting blood sugar or HbA1c test is a good idea soon.
checks.sugarTest: A simple blood sugar test at a clinic or pharmacy this year would give you peace of mind.
checks.addWaist: Add your waist size next time for a more accurate picture.
checks.pregnancy: You're pregnant, so weight-based measures aren't scored. Please follow your antenatal care team's advice.

dietitian.body: Talk about your results by video, voice or chat.

aboutBody: Your Living Score combines six areas of health into one number from 0 to 100. It's a guide to help you improve, not a medical diagnosis. If you're worried about your health, or have symptoms, please speak to a doctor.
Only you, and the experts you choose to share it with, can see these results.
methods: Body mass index: WHO classification for adults
Waist-to-height ratio: NICE guideline on overweight and obesity (2022)
Blood pressure: International Society of Hypertension global guideline (2020)
Diabetes risk: FINDRISC, Finnish Diabetes Risk Score (Lindström and Tuomilehto, 2003)
Low mood and anxiety: PHQ-2 and GAD-2 screening questions
Diet, activity and sleep: WHO healthy diet guidance and WHO physical activity guidelines (2020)
results.copied: Summary copied. Paste it into a message to your doctor.
